title: What do the numbers add up to when they climb and then fall?
description: A sum climbs from one to seven and then falls back to one, thirteen numbers in all. The book's pattern of up and down sums gives each total as the top number times itself. Keeko doubts this and says the total is fourteen, by doubling the top number.
teaching_notes: One idea: a sum that goes up to a number and back down to one gives that number times itself. Watch for students who double the top number instead of multiplying it by itself.

video_script.why: The child sees that the up and down sums of the book's pattern give square numbers, and uses it to total a longer sum without adding thirteen numbers one by one.
video_script.substitution: Use the book's pattern of up and down sums, then take the next sum in it, the one that climbs to seven.
video_script.anchor: the book's pattern of up and down sums, written line under line
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko doubles the top number seven to get fourteen, but the sum has thirteen numbers and most of them are bigger than two, so the total must be far larger.
video_script.payoff_line: Going up to seven and back down adds up to forty nine
maths_rules: up and down to n gives n x n
slip: 2 x 7 = 14, which is far less than 49
video_script.design: One idea: an up and down sum to a number is that number times itself. The book's pattern is the ground. One sum, one top number, then Keeko's doubling slip.

<bookmark mark='sum'/>The sum goes one, two, three, up to seven, and then back down to one.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>It has thirteen numbers, and adding them one by one is slow. What is the total?

narration: <bookmark mark='pattern'/>The book shows a pattern of sums that climb up and fall back down.
<bookmark mark='lines'/>Up to two and back gives four. Up to three and back gives nine. Up to four and back gives sixteen.
<bookmark mark='sq'/>Up to five gives twenty five, and up to six gives thirty six. These totals are called square numbers, and each is the top number times itself.

marks.given: the sum is written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the sum climbs from one up to seven and then falls back to one.

beats.on_screen: To find: the value of the whole sum
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the value of this whole sum.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: top number of the sum = 7

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step one, find the top number of the sum, because the pattern depends on it. Here the sum climbs to seven.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: up to a number and back down = that number x itself, so here 7 x 7

marks.rule: the rule from the pattern is written

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, use the pattern. A sum that goes up to a number and back down is that number times itself.
<bookmark mark='values'/>Here the top number is seven, so we multiply seven by seven.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Going up to seven and back down adds up to forty nine. That is the total of all thirteen numbers.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble says 14; the thirteen numbers of the sum are written in a row and most are bigger than 2; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.count: the thirteen numbers are written in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the total is fourteen. The sum goes up to seven and back down, so Keeko doubles seven.
<bookmark mark='count'/>But the sum has thirteen numbers, and most of them are bigger than two.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>Thirteen numbers like these must add up to far more than fourteen. The top number is multiplied by itself, not doubled.
